atoms.canonical_statement: The guidance aims to provide evidence-based recommendations on beta-lactam dose individualization for healthcare professionals caring for hospitalized patients treated with beta-lactams and for teams implementing dose-individualization programs.
The scope includes hospitalized patients across the age spectrum receiving systemic beta-lactam antibiotics, whether administered enterally or parenterally and regardless of infusion rate.

population.label: Hospitalized patients across the age spectrum receiving systemic beta-lactam antibiotics

atoms.canonical_statement: For this guidance, beta-lactam dose individualization requires a dosing regimen for one patient informed by measured beta-lactam concentrations from that patient; dosing based only on patient characteristics without measured concentrations is not considered truly individualized.

A multidisciplinary international panel of 19 subject-matter experts was assembled, spanning infectious diseases, critical care, pharmacy, laboratory medicine, adult and pediatric practice, pharmacometrics, and guideline methodology.
Thirteen key questions were organized into three themes: clinical impact, minimum implementation requirements, and technical/methodological considerations.

The systematic search covered Medline, Embase, Web of Science, CENTRAL, International Pharmaceutical Abstracts, ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO ICTRP, and ISRCTN, included articles in any language, and excluded animal/in-vitro studies, bioequivalence studies, case reports, and prolonged-infusion comparisons without dose-individualization assessment.
The original literature search was performed September 1, 2023 and updated July 24, 2024.
Title/abstract screening, full-text screening, and data extraction were performed independently and in duplicate, with co-chair adjudication of discrepancies.

Where sufficient high-quality evidence existed, the panel used GRADE, ROB2 for randomized trials, the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies, and an evidence-to-decision framework; otherwise, ungraded best-practice statements were developed by consensus.
Recommendations and best-practice statements were drafted and iteratively refined, approved by all panel members, and circulated to sponsoring and endorsing organizations for final approval.
The PK/PD target 100% fT>MIC means free beta-lactam concentration remains above the organism MIC for 100% of the dosing interval.
The PK/PD target 100% fT>4×MIC means free beta-lactam concentration remains above four times the organism MIC for 100% of the dosing interval.

The panel defines model-informed personalized dosing as population-PK-model-guided upfront dosing that incorporates individual covariates and measured concentrations with model-based estimation; it is intended to be proactive from the start of therapy.
The panel suggests beta-lactam antibiotic dose individualization to improve patient-centered treatment outcomes.
The panel suggests beta-lactam dose-individualization programs pursue a minimum PK/PD target of 100% fT>MIC to improve the likelihood of clinical cure.
The panel cannot recommend for or against specific PK/PD targets for mortality, microbiologic cure, or length of stay.
Loading doses and/or prolonged infusions are important to achieve a minimum PK/PD target of at least 100% fT>MIC during beta-lactam dose individualization.
For infections at sites with decreased drug distribution, such as meningitis, a higher plasma target such as 100% fT>4×MIC may be appropriate to ensure adequate target-site concentrations.
The panel cannot make a recommendation on the role of beta-lactam dose individualization to improve safety outcomes.
Adverse events, particularly neurotoxicity, should be monitored when beta-lactam dose individualization is performed.
The panel cannot make a recommendation on a specific PK target for beta-lactam dose individualization to improve safety.

Patients with acute or chronic kidney dysfunction, older age, prolonged therapy, extremes of body weight, or other risk for drug accumulation—particularly with cefepime—benefit from close beta-lactam PK monitoring to prevent accumulation and mitigate toxicity risk.
The panel supports beta-lactam dose individualization for patients with critical illness, extracorporeal support devices, kidney dysfunction, or augmented renal clearance.

Beta-lactam dose individualization may also be considered when PK abnormalities or difficult-to-treat infection are expected, including hypoalbuminemia, drug-resistant infection, inadequate response, prolonged therapy, suspected toxicity, extreme body weight, hypermetabolic states, cancer, liver failure/cirrhosis, severe burns, pregnancy, and pediatric/neonatal patients.

Successful development and implementation of a beta-lactam dose-individualization program requires a multidisciplinary stakeholder team representing institutional leadership, healthcare professionals, operational partners, regulatory support, and patients or representatives.

The optimal method for integrating beta-lactam dose individualization into clinical workflow depends on local practice structure and resources; the panel supports patterning workflows after other antibiotics such as vancomycin.
After implementation, beta-lactam dose-individualization programs should undergo iterative evaluation at regular intervals.
Plasma or serum is the preferred specimen type for beta-lactam dose individualization.
Clinical laboratories should use established best practices and a standard operating procedure for beta-lactam assay development, validation, calibration, and reporting.
Laboratory reporting should include a plan with interpretive criteria for values within, above, or below the typical range to support clinical decision-making.

The panel supports proactive MIPD using beta-lactam concentrations over traditional reactive TDM, while recognizing that either concentration-informed approach is preferred to dosing without individual concentration data.

The ideal population PK model for MIPD should be developed and validated in the population where it will be applied; otherwise model selection should consider source population, sample size, covariates, sample density, and validation methods.

Before changing a dose when observed concentrations disagree with model predictions, the panel supports a systematic evaluation of model appropriateness, input accuracy, and stability of patient physiology and clinical status.

For dose individualization, the panel supports use of a laboratory-defined organism MIC; when the reported MIC is in the susceptible range, the higher numerical value of the susceptibility breakpoint or ECV/ECOFF should guide the PK/PD target rather than the isolate-reported MIC.
When the isolate MIC exceeds the susceptibility breakpoint or ECV/ECOFF, clinicians should consider the effectiveness and safety of alternative antibiotics or combinations.

If no other safe antibiotic exists to which the organism is susceptible, one doubling dilution above the isolate MIC may be considered for beta-lactam dose individualization, provided the dose required to reach that threshold is safe in humans.
Validated measurements of free beta-lactam concentrations are preferred when available.
When free beta-lactam concentration measurement is unavailable, the panel supports estimating free concentrations from total concentrations using published protein-binding values.
The guidance meta-analysis reported a non-significant lower odds of mortality with beta-lactam dose individualization versus standard care (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.54–1.06).

population.label: Studies included in the guidance meta-analysis of beta-lactam dose individualization versus standard care

atoms.canonical_statement: When restricted to randomized trials, the guidance reported an odds ratio for mortality of 0.91 (95% CI 0.62–1.33) for dose individualization versus standard care.

population.label: Randomized trials included in the guidance mortality synthesis

atoms.canonical_statement: The guidance meta-analysis reported higher odds of clinical cure with beta-lactam dose individualization versus standard care (OR 1.99, 95% CI 1.54–2.56).

population.label: Studies included in the guidance meta-analysis of beta-lactam dose individualization versus standard care

atoms.canonical_statement: The guidance meta-analysis reported no statistically significant increase in microbiologic cure with beta-lactam dose individualization versus standard care (OR 1.42, 95% CI 0.73–2.76).

population.label: Studies included in the guidance meta-analysis of beta-lactam dose individualization versus standard care

atoms.canonical_statement: Beta-lactam dose individualization did not reduce hospital or ICU length of stay in the guidance synthesis; Bayesian posterior probabilities of reduction were 48%–59% for hospital stay and 52%–59% for ICU stay.
Across studies, achieving a study-defined beta-lactam PK/PD target was not associated with significantly different mortality (OR 1.45, 95% CI 0.89–2.38).

atoms.canonical_statement: In a high-quality retrospective cohort, clinical cure occurred in 183/225 patients achieving 100% fT>MIC versus 130/181 who did not, corresponding to OR 1.71 (95% CI 1.07–2.72).

population.label: Critically ill patients in the Wu et al. retrospective cohort summarized by the guidance

atoms.canonical_statement: The overall effect estimate for clinical cure with study-defined PK/PD target attainment was OR 2.16 (95% CI 0.89–5.29).

atoms.canonical_statement: The guidance safety meta-analysis found no significant difference in neurotoxicity between individualized dosing and standard care (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.45–2.00).

population.label: Studies comparing beta-lactam dose individualization with standard care for safety outcomes

atoms.canonical_statement: The guidance reported no significant difference in nephrotoxicity with individualized dosing versus standard care (pooled OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.43–1.61).

population.label: Studies comparing beta-lactam dose individualization with standard care for safety outcomes

atoms.canonical_statement: The guidance reported no significant difference in hepatotoxicity with individualized dosing versus standard care (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.53–1.54).

population.label: Studies comparing beta-lactam dose individualization with standard care for safety outcomes

atoms.canonical_statement: For a broad composite of any safety event, the guidance meta-analysis reported OR 1.04 (95% CI 0.60–1.81) for individualized dosing versus standard care.

atoms.canonical_statement: In a higher-quality study summarized by the guidance, neurological deterioration occurred in 75.7% (28/38) of patients with excessive exposure defined as Cmin/MIC ≥12.4 versus 33.3% (24/81) below that threshold.

atoms.canonical_statement: The panel notes that cefepime concentration-dependent neurotoxicity in adults is most commonly reported when trough concentrations exceed approximately 20–35 mg/L; thresholds for other beta-lactams are less well established.

The clinical-outcome evidence included few randomized trials, used heterogeneous outcome definitions, and produced imprecise or inconsistent estimates, leading to low or very-low certainty for several outcomes.

PK/PD target studies used heterogeneous targets, infusion strategies, and often assumed susceptibility breakpoints or ECV/ECOFF rather than measured pathogen-specific MICs, contributing to variability and imprecision.
Safety estimates were limited by small numbers of studies, indirectness, heterogeneous toxicity definitions, and variable effect sizes, resulting in low confidence.

Clear toxicodynamic thresholds in acutely ill patients remain uncertain because of confounding by kidney dysfunction and illness severity, heterogeneous exposure definitions, inconsistent safety assessment, and generally lower-quality evidence.
A comprehensive evaluation of the health-economic impact of beta-lactam dose individualization is lacking.

Most evidence underlying the guidance was obtained in resource-rich environments, limiting direct transferability to resource-limited settings with different patient populations, drug use, susceptibility patterns, staffing, software, and assay access.

Pediatric and neonatal beta-lactam dose individualization is constrained by age-dependent PK, fewer available pediatric population-PK models and MIPD implementations, and difficulty powering clinical outcome studies because mortality is lower than in adults.
In adults, augmented renal clearance is typically defined in the guidance as creatinine clearance greater than 130 mL/min/1.73 m².

The panel states that most published beta-lactam assays use plasma or serum; plasma can be processed immediately without waiting for clotting, which is relevant because beta-lactams may be unstable at room temperature.
When selecting an MIPD population-PK model, the panel identifies body-size and kidney-function metrics as minimum essential covariates for beta-lactams, especially in children or body-size extremes.

For model-prediction discordance, if systematic review of model choice, inputs, and patient changes does not resolve the problem, the guidance supports alternative models and, if necessary, non-model-based exposure assessment.

The MIC target-selection algorithm first compares the patient-specific MIC with the susceptibility breakpoint and ECV/ECOFF; if the MIC is not above those thresholds, the higher of the breakpoint or ECV/ECOFF is used as the comparator for PK/PD target selection.

In children and neonates, developmental physiology causes major age-related changes in beta-lactam disposition; after organ maturation, size-normalized clearance can be more rapid than in adults and increase underexposure risk.

The panel concludes that current evidence suggests potential effectiveness benefits of beta-lactam dose individualization, especially for clinical cure, while high-quality clinical trials remain limited and consistent evidence of harm has not been demonstrated.
The guidance is not intended to mandate universal implementation; implementation should be tailored to local resources, assay access, MIPD tools, and multidisciplinary expertise.

Future research priorities include defining optimal PK/PD targets in well-defined populations, evaluating patient-centered effectiveness and safety, identifying heterogeneity of treatment effects and responsive subgroups, assessing microbiome effects, and evaluating cost-effectiveness.

Pharmacotherapy Publications, Inc. (now the ACCP Foundation, Ltd.) supported development of the consensus statement; the methodology section states that no funding or influence was derived from the healthcare industry.

schema_gaps: The LiteratureAtom schema has no dedicated guideline_recommendation or best_practice_statement atom kind. Consensus recommendations are represented as author_conclusion atoms with descriptive tags.

The source is consensus guidance rather than primary literature. Quantitative evidence atoms are explicitly tagged secondary_reported_result and anchored to the guidance, not to the underlying primary studies.
extraction_limitations: No companion PDFs were listed in the task. The article cites Supporting Information Appendices S1-S5 and Tables S1-S8, but these were not provided and were not silently substituted from the web.
Bibliography entries were extracted separately to Markdown and were not atomized as evidence.
Recommendation strength/certainty are preserved in statement text and tags where explicitly reported; no unreported grades were inferred.
